explanation: Fires on the token 'but' and 'And'/'and'. It fires most when the token starts a new sentence or paragraph after code or a blank line ('But it doesn't work', 'And when I call'), in the license line 'but WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY', and also on 'but' as a word-piece ('butler', 'butyl', 'butts', 'Butland'). Mid-sentence 'and'/'or' conjunctions in prose give only weak to moderate activation.

A mixture. The strongest hit is the squared exponent '2' in math formulas (a_1^2, b^2). Moderate activations come on housing and real-estate words (bedroom, sq. ft, Single Family, homes, lofts, cottage, at home) and on scattered phrasal or storage words ('laid out', 'sitting on', 'locked away', 'stored'). No single cue predicts it well.

Fires on mid-word subword fragments, mostly in non-English text (Finnish, French, Portuguese) and in personal names (K-ait-lyn, El-way, Kl-uber, T-yr-anny). It also fires on some auxiliaries like 'a', 'has', 'have', 'avait' and on 'nearly'. The common thread is loosely 'continuing a word or name in less-common orthography'.

Mixed. It fires on subword fragments inside rare words or names (Cour-ser-a, circ-ovirus, Pan-try, Ram-írez, cran-ial, Cer-ro) and on the preposition in idioms like 'something to do with', 'nothing to do with' and 'conflicts of law'. It also fires on some digits in addresses or codes.

Fires on content nouns or noun pieces that end a noun phrase, especially group or political actors (al Qaeda, Kurdish fighters, rebels, Democrats, agent) and concrete objects or name endings (pretzels, Sandpipers, sculpture, playground, blade). The strongest hit is 'harboring a fugitive'. There is no clear unifying semantic theme.

Fires on function words that start or continue a common fixed phrase or construction: 'from' in 'vary, from X to Y', 'once in a lifetime', 'in awhile', 'If you can/want', 'at least', 'a copy of which', 'you can redistribute', 'tending to'. The context predicts the next words strongly. It is a generic phrase-continuation detector with no clear semantics.

Fires most strongly on 'other' in 'among other things/others'. It also fires on several unrelated tokens: the '{' in '\begin{array}', the capitalization pieces of Xcode/NEON, and comment markers ('#', '//') that start a new comment paragraph in license or config headers.

Fires on the subword 'os' or 's' piece that joins two parts of a compound word, especially Greek/Latin scientific compounds (psych-os-ocial, olig-os-accharide, som-atos-ensory, proct-os-igmoid, fluor-os-copy) and hyphen- or slash-joined compounds (free-spirit, life/school, aftershave). The token is a stem-joining piece starting with 's' in the middle of a word.

Fires mainly inside software license headers: 'with' in 'in compliance with the License', 'LICENSE' or 'license' in 'see the LICENSE file', and 'distributed', 'granted,'. It also fires weakly or moderately on a few unrelated nouns (option, border, storage, region).

Fires on the subword 'ch' (or Cyrillic 'Ч/ч') at the start of a word part, especially right after a hyphen or slash ('-ch' in life-changing, multi-chamber, low-chlorophyll, Editor-in-Chief; '/ch' in suspension/chassis, oxide/chitosan) or after a space ('Ch'allenged, 'ch'atty). Other similar digraph onsets (h, dich, ech) give weaker activation.

Fires mainly on 'governing' in the license boilerplate 'See the License for the specific language governing permissions'. More broadly it fires on participles or prepositions that link a noun to its agent or source ('coming from', 'occurred in', 'played by', 'constructed', 'secreted', 'produced by').

Mixed. It fires on digits inside statistics or numeric values (.26, < 30, 57.2%, width=50, 1965), on nouns after counts or modifiers ('14 patients', 'overall record', 'many years'), and on miscellaneous words like 'manually', 'null' and 'array'. There is no single clear concept.

Fires on the preposition 'by' (and sometimes 'from') that introduces the agent after a passive verb or nominalization: 'published by', 'appointed by', 'banned by', 'endorsed by', 'nomination by', 'status from'. Other prepositions and 'that' after verbs give weaker activation.

Fires on web and online-platform tokens: '.com' in URLs (strongest, e.g. youtube.com, medium.com), platform names (YouTube, Reddit, Twitter), coupon or rewards words, 'Forwarded by' in email headers, and API pieces like '.auth'. It also has some unrelated weaker hits ('surprise', 'term').

Fires on subword fragments inside proper names and foreign or transliterated words, especially place names, organizations and political parties (Derbyshire Min-ers, Dou-ma, Gap-m-inder, Peoples Party, Samajw-adi, Hogs-me-ade, Muj-ah-ideen) and some technical terms (gnot-ob-iotic, intr-ab-ody). It fires on pieces in the middle of a name rather than on whole common words.

Fires on determiners and articles, especially the article right after a verb or preposition in Romance-language text (French/Spanish/Portuguese 'la', 'o', 'da', 'esa'). In English it fires on 'such a', 'between a', 'along with this', 'investigate this'. It is essentially a determiner detector.

Fires on separators between items in a list or parameter list: commas between function parameters or type arguments, 'and' or 'with' joining coordinated noun phrases, '@param', and 'v.' in legal case captions. The strongest hit is 'arrays and an integer n as parameters'.

Fires on function words or modifiers that come right after a descriptive or classifying head, in factual or biomedical descriptions: 'species of', 'genus of', 'model of', 'patients with', 'weakness of right side', 'revealed some', 'a distinctive', 'a lower'. It responds to the slot just after a taxonomic or clinical-description word and is broad.

Fires on the first word after a sentence-opening framing phrase: ''s' in 'this week's'/'today's', 'it' or 'we' after an introductory clause ('When loaded in a page, it'; 'In any case we'), and 'of' in 'In the theory of', 'For assessment of'. It marks where the main clause begins after a front-loaded adverbial or prepositional phrase.

Mixed. It fires on assorted tokens inside proper names, technical strings, URL parts ('://'), product names (Atari 7800), the 'in' in degree/program phrases (MA in, candidate in), and directional words. No common theme is evident.

Fires on a wide variety of tokens in technical, code and foreign-language text: template parameters (size_t), separators (':' in ARNs, ',' in [[n,k,d]], '://'), prepositions in technical questions, and Czech, Hungarian or Italian word endings. There is no identifiable unifying feature.
